options.C: The pages were printed in the university town of Wittenberg.
options.D: The captions are in German, not Latin.

practice.explanation: Most books for scholars and churchmen were written in Latin. German text, together with simple pictures, made the pamphlet's message clear to readers who knew little or no Latin.

whyNot.A: Scholars and ordinary people alike knew stories about Christ, so this does not show who the audience was.
whyNot.B: The triple crown shows that the figure is the pope. It does not show who the pamphlet was meant for.
whyNot.C: Wittenberg was the home of Luther's university. Where a book was printed does not show who was meant to read it.

practice.hint: What language did university scholars and church officials usually write in?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the main purpose of the edict?

options.A: to call a church council that would judge Luther's ideas fairly
options.B: to let each German prince decide which religion his lands would follow
options.C: to brand Luther a heretic and forbid the reading of his books
options.D: to reform the sale of indulgences that Luther had criticized

practice.explanation: After Luther refused to take back his writings at Worms in April 1521, Charles V declared him an outlaw. The edict forbade anyone to buy, read, copy, or print his books.

whyNot.A: The edict calls Luther "a notorious and stiffnecked heretic" and bans his books. It does not ask a council to decide.
whyNot.B: The edict orders "each and all" to obey its ban on Luther's books. It gives princes no choice about religion.
whyNot.D: The edict defends the Church against Luther. It says nothing about changing how indulgences were sold.

practice.hint: Look at article 29. What does it forbid people to do?

practice.stem: Charles V's ability to enforce the edict in Germany in the 1520s and 1530s was most weakened by which of the following?

options.A: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
options.B: The outbreak of the Thirty Years' War
options.C: Wars with France and the Ottoman Empire
options.D: The Dutch revolt against Spanish rule

practice.explanation: Charles V spent years fighting France and the Ottoman Turks, who attacked Vienna in 1529. He needed help from the German princes, even Lutheran ones. So he could not crush the Lutherans.

whyNot.A: The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588, under Charles's son Philip II, decades after the 1520s and 1530s.
whyNot.B: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, more than sixty years after Charles V gave up his thrones in 1555–1556.
whyNot.D: The Dutch revolt against Spain began in 1568, under Philip II.

practice.hint: The edict lists the many lands Charles ruled. Which enemies threatened those lands in the 1520s and 1530s?

practice.stem: Despite the edict, Lutheranism first gained lasting legal recognition in the Holy Roman Empire through which of the following?

options.A: The Peace of Augsburg
options.B: The Peace of Westphalia
options.C: The Edict of Nantes
options.D: The Edict of Restitution

practice.explanation: In the Peace of Augsburg (1555), the empire's rulers agreed that each prince could choose Catholicism or Lutheranism for his lands. The edict had tried to stamp out Luther's faith, but now it was legal in the empire.

whyNot.B: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) came almost a century later. It confirmed the earlier settlement and added Calvinism to the faiths a ruler could choose.
whyNot.C: The Edict of Nantes (1598) was issued by King Henry IV of France. It gave rights to French Protestants, not to Lutherans in the empire.
whyNot.D: The Edict of Restitution (1629) ordered Protestants to give back church lands they had taken. It tried to undo Protestant gains, not protect them.

practice.hint: Which agreement ended the religious fighting in Germany in the 1550s?

practice.stem: Which of the following best explains the change in the number of works printed in German from 1517 to 1523?

options.A: The printing press with movable type was first invented in Germany during these years.
options.B: Italian printers such as Aldus Manutius began printing ancient Greek and Latin works.
options.C: Luther and other writers published many pamphlets in German about the religious dispute.
options.D: Emperor Charles V paid printers to publish books in German to unite his empire.

practice.explanation: After 1517 Luther wrote many short works in German, and printers rushed to reprint them. Supporters and opponents answered with pamphlets of their own. The number of German works printed rose from 81 in 1517 to 944 in 1523.

whyNot.A: Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable type in Mainz in the 1450s, more than sixty years earlier.
whyNot.B: Aldus Manutius began printing Greek and Latin classics in Venice in the 1490s. The chart counts works printed in German.
whyNot.D: Charles V's Edict of Worms (1521) banned the printing of Luther's books.

practice.hint: What famous dispute began in Germany in 1517?

practice.stem: The rise in printing shown in the chart depended most on which earlier development?

options.A: The spread of printing presses with movable type
options.B: The founding of the Society of Jesus
options.C: The wars between the Habsburgs and France over Italy
options.D: The Treaty of Tordesillas's division of lands

practice.explanation: Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type press, first used in Mainz in the 1450s, spread to many cities and towns across Europe by 1500. It made books and pamphlets much faster and cheaper to produce.

whyNot.B: The Society of Jesus (the Jesuits) was founded in 1540, after these years, and it worked against the spread of Protestant ideas.
whyNot.C: The wars in Italy (1494–1559) were fought over land and power. They had nothing to do with how books were made.
whyNot.D: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly reached lands between Spain and Portugal. It had nothing to do with printing.

practice.hint: Which choice made it possible to make many copies of a pamphlet quickly?

practice.stem: A historian wants to use the chart to argue that Luther's writings caused the rise in German printing. Which additional information would the historian most need?

options.A: the number of works printed in Latin in German lands in the years before 1513
options.B: the number of printing presses at work in Italy and France in the year 1523
options.C: the number of people living in German cities and towns in the year 1450
options.D: how many works each year were by Luther or about the religious dispute

practice.explanation: The chart counts German works "on any subject." To tie the rise to Luther, a historian would need to know how many works were by Luther or about the religious fight. Later studies found that Luther wrote a large share of them.

whyNot.A: Latin works from before 1513 come before the change the historian wants to explain, and the chart is about German works.
whyNot.B: Presses in Italy and France would not show what was being printed in German.
whyNot.C: Population figures from 1450 are from long before the change and say nothing about what was printed.

practice.hint: The note says the chart counts works "on any subject." What does that leave unclear?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the beliefs expressed in the articles?

options.A: Christians should obey rulers who protect the true faith and should help them punish heretics.
options.B: Infants should be baptized so that they can belong to the church community from their birth.
options.C: True Christians should keep apart from the world and refuse to use the sword or swear oaths.
options.D: Church leaders should be chosen by Christian princes in order to keep good order in the church.

practice.explanation: The Anabaptists who met at Schleitheim wanted a church made up only of adult believers. They baptized only people who had chosen to repent and believe. They would not use the sword, swear oaths, or serve as magistrates.

whyNot.A: The articles say the sword is "outside the perfection of Christ" and that a Christian "is not permitted to be a magistrate."
whyNot.B: The articles call infant baptism "the supreme abomination of the Roman Pontif" and baptize only people who repent and believe.
whyNot.D: The articles want Christians kept apart from rulers' power. They would not want princes to choose church leaders.

practice.hint: Look at the Sixth and Seventh articles. What will these Christians refuse to do?

practice.stem: Beliefs like those in the articles most directly led to which of the following?

options.A: The adoption of Anabaptist beliefs by the city council of Zurich in 1527
options.B: Recognition of Anabaptists in the Peace of Augsburg
options.C: The Council of Trent's decision to end infant baptism
options.D: Persecution by both Catholic and Protestant rulers

practice.explanation: Rulers feared people who would not swear oaths, fight as soldiers, or baptize babies. Both Catholic and Protestant rulers jailed, drowned, and burned Anabaptists. Michael Sattler, who led the Schleitheim meeting, was put to death in May 1527.

whyNot.A: Zurich made Anabaptism a crime. In January 1527 the city drowned the Anabaptist leader Felix Manz.
whyNot.B: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) allowed only two faiths: Catholic and Lutheran.
whyNot.C: The Council of Trent upheld infant baptism.

practice.hint: How would rulers who depended on oaths and soldiers react to these beliefs?

practice.stem: In which of the following ways did the Anabaptists' view of baptism differ from that of Luther and Zwingli?

options.A: The Anabaptists kept infant baptism, while Luther and Zwingli baptized adult believers instead.
options.B: The Anabaptists baptized only believers old enough to repent, while Luther and Zwingli kept infant baptism.
options.C: The Anabaptists required bishops to baptize, while Luther and Zwingli let any pastor baptize.
options.D: The Anabaptists baptized in Latin, while Luther and Zwingli baptized in German.

practice.explanation: Luther and Zwingli kept baptizing babies. The Anabaptists baptized only people who had turned from sin and believed. Their enemies said they baptized people a second time, so they called them Anabaptists, which means rebaptizers.

whyNot.A: This reverses the two sides. The articles exclude "all baptism of infants."
whyNot.C: Anabaptists had no bishops. Their disagreement with Luther and Zwingli was about who should be baptized, not who performed it.
whyNot.D: The dispute was about who should be baptized, not about the language used.

practice.hint: Look at the First article. Who does it say should be baptized?

practice.stem: Taken together, the two sources best support which of the following conclusions about Geneva under Calvin?

options.A: The city councils left religious questions to the ministers and elders alone.
options.B: Church and city government worked together to supervise people's lives.
options.C: Catholics were free to attend Mass in Geneva as long as they paid a small fine.
options.D: The pope's bishops chose the elders who watched over the conduct and morals of Geneva's people.

practice.explanation: In Calvin's Geneva, elders chosen from the city councils watched over every part of the city. The consistory of ministers and elders scolded people who did wrong. The city council could fine them or put them in prison.

whyNot.A: Source 1 says the elders are chosen from the city's councils, and both sources send stubborn offenders to "the council."
whyNot.C: Source 2 sends people who go to Mass before the council, which may punish them "by imprisonment or special fines."
whyNot.D: Geneva had broken with the pope in 1536. Source 1 says the elders are chosen from Geneva's own councils.

practice.hint: In both sources, who punishes people who will not obey the elders?

practice.stem: The rules in Source 2 best illustrate which of the following developments of the 1500s?

options.A: Religious toleration in Protestant states
options.B: Enclosure of common lands for private farming
options.C: Regulation of public morals by local governments
options.D: Divine-right absolutism

practice.explanation: In the 1500s, many towns, both Catholic and Protestant, made rules against swearing, drinking, gambling, and dancing. The Reformation weakened the old church courts, so town leaders did more of this work.

whyNot.A: Source 2 punishes people for owning rosaries or going to Mass. That is the opposite of toleration.
whyNot.B: Enclosure was the fencing of common land for private farming, mostly in England. These rules are about worship and behavior.
whyNot.D: Divine-right absolutism means kings claiming unlimited power from God, as Louis XIV did in the late 1600s. Geneva was a self-governing city.

practice.hint: What kinds of behavior do the rules in Source 2 punish?

practice.stem: Rules like those in Source 2 are most similar to which later development?

options.A: Puritan limits on Sunday games and theaters in England
options.B: The French Revolution's Civil Constitution of the Clergy
options.C: Louis XIV's building of the palace of Versailles
options.D: Voltaire's calls for religious toleration

practice.explanation: English Puritans shared many of Calvin's beliefs. They worked to make daily life more godly and opposed Sunday sports and festivals. In 1642 Parliament closed London's theaters.

whyNot.B: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790) put the French clergy under the state. It was about church government, not people's games or behavior.
whyNot.C: Versailles was a royal palace built to display Louis XIV's power, not a set of moral rules.
whyNot.D: Voltaire called for religious toleration, the opposite of punishing people for how they worship.

practice.hint: Which group in a later century shared many of Calvin's beliefs?

practice.stem: Both sources reflect which of the following?

options.A: Parliament's right to choose the bishops of the Church of England
options.B: An agreement between the crown and the papacy to share church authority
options.C: The English monarch's control over the Church of England in place of the pope
options.D: The English clergy's power to approve or reject the monarch's laws

practice.explanation: In 1534 Parliament named Henry VIII "the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England." In 1559 Elizabeth I's oath again rejected any "foreign" church authority. In both, the monarch, not the pope, controlled the English church.

whyNot.A: Both sources give church authority to the monarch. Parliament passes the laws, but neither source says Parliament chooses bishops.
whyNot.B: Both sources reject "foreign" authority, meaning the pope's. Neither shares power with Rome.
whyNot.D: Source 1 says the clergy "recognized" the king as head, and Source 2 makes clergy swear an oath to the queen.

practice.hint: Who holds church authority in each source, and who is shut out?

practice.stem: Which development between 1534 and 1559 most directly explains why a new act was needed in 1559?

options.A: Mary I's return to papal authority
options.B: Henry VIII's closing of the monasteries
options.C: Edward VI's Book of Common Prayer
options.D: The Pilgrimage of Grace

practice.explanation: Mary I, a Catholic, became queen in 1553. At her urging, Parliament canceled Henry VIII's laws against the pope and brought back the pope's authority. When Elizabeth I became queen in 1558, a new act was needed to break with Rome again.

whyNot.B: Henry VIII closed the monasteries between 1536 and 1540 and took their lands. This strengthened royal control of the church, so it did not create a need for a new act.
whyNot.C: Edward VI's Book of Common Prayer (1549) made English worship more Protestant. It did not undo the monarch's headship of the church.
whyNot.D: The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) was a northern rising against Henry's religious changes. Henry crushed it, and the 1534 Act stayed in force.

practice.hint: Which choice would have cancelled the 1534 Act?

practice.stem: Source 1 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Henry VIII's quarrel with the pope over his marriage to Catherine of Aragon
options.B: Elizabeth I's conflict with Catholic Spain over control of the rebellious Netherlands
options.C: Puritan demands that England adopt a church run by elders on Calvin's model
options.D: England's alliance with the Holy Roman Emperor against the Ottoman Turks

practice.explanation: Pope Clement VII refused to end Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon. In 1533 Henry married Anne Boleyn, and Parliament cut the English church's ties to Rome. The Act of Supremacy of 1534 made the king head of the church.

whyNot.B: Elizabeth's conflict with Spain came decades later, in the 1580s.
whyNot.C: English Puritans pushed for a church like Calvin's mostly after 1559, under Elizabeth.
whyNot.D: Henry VIII and Charles V were at odds in these years. Charles was Catherine of Aragon's nephew, and his power made the pope unwilling to grant Henry's request.

practice.hint: Why did Henry VIII want to break with the pope in the early 1530s?

practice.stem: Marguerite's account is especially useful to historians of the massacre because she

options.A: was a Huguenot leader who organized the defense of the Protestants of Paris that night
options.B: was inside the royal palace and close to the family members who ordered the killings
options.C: wrote her account on the day after the massacre, while the details were still fresh
options.D: had no ties to either religious side and could report events without bias

practice.explanation: Marguerite was the daughter of Catherine de' Medici and the sister of King Charles IX. That night she was inside the royal palace, close to the people who ordered the killings. She also saw some of the violence herself.

whyNot.A: Marguerite says the Huguenots distrusted her "because I was a Catholic." She was not one of their leaders.
whyNot.C: The attribution says she wrote in the 1590s, more than twenty years later.
whyNot.D: She was a Catholic married to a Huguenot and the sister of the king, so she had ties to both sides.

practice.hint: Where was Marguerite that night, and who were her relatives?

practice.stem: A historian should be most cautious about Marguerite's claim that King Charles acted only after he was "convinced of the intentions of the Huguenots" because Marguerite

options.A: was a Protestant who wanted to blame the Catholic king for the killings
options.B: was writing about her own brother and mother, whose reputations her account protects
options.C: was too young at the time to understand anything about politics at court
options.D: was writing for Huguenot readers who expected the king and his mother to be praised

practice.explanation: Marguerite calls her brother "a prince of great prudence." She says he acted only after he was "convinced" the Huguenots were a threat. As part of the royal family, she had reasons to make her brother and mother look less to blame.

whyNot.A: Marguerite was a Catholic, and she calls King Charles "a prince of great prudence."
whyNot.C: Marguerite was nineteen and newly married. She understood the danger well enough to fear for her life that night.
whyNot.D: Huguenots blamed the king and his mother for the massacre. They would not have wanted to read praise of King Charles.

practice.hint: Who was King Charles to Marguerite, and who was "the Queen his mother"?

practice.stem: The violence described in the passage most directly led to which of the following?

options.A: The Edict of Nantes
options.B: The expulsion of the Jesuits from France
options.C: A Spanish conquest of France
options.D: Renewed civil war in France

practice.explanation: After the massacre, the Huguenots took up arms again. Some Protestant writers argued that people could resist a king who acted like a tyrant. The French Wars of Religion went on until 1598.

whyNot.A: The Edict of Nantes came in 1598, after more than twenty-five more years of war. It was not a direct result of 1572.
whyNot.B: France expelled the Jesuits only briefly in the 1590s and again in 1764, for reasons that had nothing to do with this massacre.
whyNot.C: Philip II of Spain sent troops to help the Catholic League in the 1590s, but Spain never conquered France.

practice.hint: Did the massacre end the conflict or make it worse?

practice.stem: In the first paragraph, Montaigne argues that

options.A: the Huguenots' cause in the civil war is more just than the Catholic cause
options.B: even good men on the better side can be driven by zeal to injustice
options.C: the civil war is caused mainly by greedy nobles who merely pretend to care about religion
options.D: the king should force the French people to return to the ancient religion

practice.explanation: Montaigne, a Catholic, thinks the Catholic side is right. Still, he warns that zeal without "moderation" leads even good people to "unjust and violent" actions.

whyNot.A: Montaigne says the "soundest cause" is the one that keeps "the ancient religion," the Catholic faith.
whyNot.C: Montaigne mentions people who "only make a pretence" of religion, but he sets them aside to discuss sincere "good men" carried away by passion.
whyNot.D: Montaigne criticizes "counsels that are unjust and violent." His essay favors calming the conflict, not forcing belief.

practice.hint: What does Montaigne say about "good intentions" carried on "without moderation"?

practice.stem: Montaigne's views in the passage are most similar to those of which group?

options.A: The Catholic League
options.B: The politiques
options.C: The Jesuits
options.D: The Anabaptists

practice.explanation: The politiques were French leaders, mostly Catholic. They cared more about peace and keeping France whole than about making everyone follow one church. Montaigne notes that "our kings" use liberty of conscience "to extinguish" civil conflict, and he accepts their choice.

whyNot.A: The Catholic League, led by the Guise family, wanted to wipe out Protestantism in France and refused to accept a Protestant king.
whyNot.C: The Jesuits worked to win Protestants back to the Catholic Church. They did not favor liberty of conscience.
whyNot.D: Anabaptists separated from the world and refused to hold office. Montaigne writes as a loyal subject who accepts the choice of "our kings" to calm the conflict.

practice.hint: Which group cared most about ending the civil war, even at the cost of religious unity?

practice.stem: Montaigne's point that toleration could "mollify and appease" people was most fully put into practice by which later measure?

options.A: The Peace of Augsburg
options.B: The decrees of the Council of Trent
options.C: The Edict of Nantes
options.D: The English Act of Supremacy

practice.explanation: In 1598 King Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes. It let Huguenots worship in many places and hold public office. This brought peace to France, while Catholicism stayed the main religion.

whyNot.A: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) came before this essay and applied to the Holy Roman Empire. It let rulers, not individuals, choose the religion of their lands.
whyNot.B: The Council of Trent (1545–1563) defined Catholic teaching against the Protestants. It did not grant toleration.
whyNot.D: The Act of Supremacy made the English monarch head of the Church of England. It did not grant freedom of worship.

practice.hint: Which measure was issued by a French king after this essay was published in 1580?

practice.stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following features of the Thirty Years' War?

options.A: Soldiers living off the land and abusing the civilians in their path
options.B: Large naval battles fought between Sweden and the emperor in the Baltic Sea
options.C: Peasant armies rising against their lords to demand an end to serfdom
options.D: Well-paid professional armies that were forbidden to take civilians' goods

practice.explanation: Armies in the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) often went unpaid and took food and goods from the people around them. Villages were robbed and burned, and peasants were tortured to reveal hidden valuables.

whyNot.B: Most fighting in the war took place on land in the Holy Roman Empire. The troopers here raid a farm.
whyNot.C: That describes the German Peasants' War of 1525. In the passage, soldiers attack peasants.
whyNot.D: Most soldiers were mercenaries who often went unpaid and lived by plunder, as the troopers in the passage do.

practice.hint: Who are the victims in the passage, and who are the attackers?

practice.stem: Which of the following should a historian consider when using this passage as evidence of conditions during the war?

options.A: It was written by a Swedish general who wanted to excuse his army's actions.
options.B: It was written on the emperor's orders to blame the Protestants for the war.
options.C: It was written before the war began, so it could do no more than predict what war would be like.
options.D: It is a novel, though its author had served as a soldier in the war.

practice.explanation: A novel can mix real events with made-up or exaggerated scenes. But Grimmelshausen served as a soldier in the war, so his story shows things that really happened to German villagers.

whyNot.A: Grimmelshausen was a German writer, not a Swedish general, and the passage condemns the troopers' cruelty.
whyNot.B: Nothing shows the emperor ordered the book. It describes soldiers' cruelty without praising either side.
whyNot.C: The novel was published in 1668, twenty years after the war ended in 1648.

practice.hint: Read the attribution. What kind of writing is this, and when was it published?

practice.stem: Destruction like that described in the passage most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: Rapid growth of German cities during the war
options.B: The end of serfdom in central Europe by 1650
options.C: A sharp fall in population in many German lands
options.D: Germany's rise as a leading colonial power

practice.explanation: During the Thirty Years' War, fighting, hunger, and disease killed millions of people. Some regions of Germany lost a third or more of their people.

whyNot.A: War, hunger, and disease made many German towns shrink, and cities such as Magdeburg were destroyed.
whyNot.B: Serfdom continued in much of central and eastern Europe until the 1800s.
whyNot.D: The German states had almost no overseas colonies in this period. Spain, Portugal, the Dutch, England, and France led overseas expansion.

practice.hint: What happens to a farming region when its animals, tools, and homes are destroyed?

practice.stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: The Protestant belief that each Christian may interpret Scripture alone
options.B: The intense personal piety and mysticism of the Catholic Reformation
options.C: The humanist interest in reviving ancient Greek and Roman writers
options.D: The selling of indulgences to raise money for churches in Rome

practice.explanation: Teresa of Ávila reformed the Carmelite order of nuns and wrote about prayer and visions. Her deep, emotional faith was part of the Catholic revival of the 1500s. The Church later made her a saint.

whyNot.A: Teresa was a Catholic nun who grieved for "the Lutherans" as "lost souls" and told women to rely on their confessors.
whyNot.C: Teresa writes about a vision of an angel and her love of God, not about classical authors.
whyNot.D: Teresa says nothing about indulgences. Church leaders of her time were working to end the abuses linked to them.

practice.hint: What kind of religious experience does Teresa describe?

practice.stem: Teresa's comments about women in the last paragraph suggest that she

options.A: believed that women should be allowed to become priests and preach in churches
options.B: accepted male clergy's guidance while also claiming that women had special spiritual gifts
options.C: thought women should stay away from prayer and leave religion to learned men
options.D: rejected the authority of priests and confessors because she believed God spoke to her directly

practice.explanation: Teresa repeats Peter of Alcantara's view that "women made greater progress" in prayer than men. Yet she also tells women to rely on an experienced confessor. She worked within the Church's rules for women.

whyNot.A: Teresa says women should "go to their confessor," who was a male priest. She does not call for women to become priests.
whyNot.C: Teresa says God gives "these graces" to more women than men, so she wants women to pray.
whyNot.D: Teresa says women should go to a confessor who is "a man of experience," so she accepts confessors' authority.

practice.hint: Find two things Teresa says about women: one about their gifts, and one about whom they should turn to for advice.

practice.stem: The vision described in the first two paragraphs is the subject of which later work of art?

options.A: Bernini's The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
options.B: Michelangelo's David
options.C: Bruegel's painting The Peasant Wedding
options.D: Rembrandt's The Night Watch

practice.explanation: Bernini made a marble statue of this vision between 1647 and 1652. It shows an angel about to pierce Teresa's heart with a golden spear. Its drama and strong feeling are typical of Baroque art in Catholic churches.

whyNot.B: Michelangelo's David (1501–1504) shows the Bible hero David and was finished before Teresa was born.
whyNot.C: Bruegel's painting (about 1567) shows a village wedding feast, not a religious vision.
whyNot.D: Rembrandt's The Night Watch (1642) is a group portrait of members of a Dutch city militia.

practice.hint: Which of these artists worked for the Catholic Church in Rome in the 1600s?

practice.stem: According to Ranke, the Jesuits gained influence mainly by

options.A: leading Catholic armies against the Protestant princes of Germany
options.B: running free schools and serving as confessors and spiritual advisers
options.C: selling indulgences to pay for new schools and churches in Italy
options.D: translating the Bible into the everyday languages of Europe

practice.explanation: Ranke says the Jesuits built well-run schools that charged no fees. They also took control of "the confessional" and "the direction of consciences." Their former students became cardinals and city leaders.

whyNot.A: Ranke says the order arose "in strictest alliance" with church power, but he credits schools and the confessional, not armies.
whyNot.C: Ranke says the Jesuits "taught gratis," which means free of charge.
whyNot.D: Ranke does not mention Bible translation. He stresses their schools and their work as confessors.

practice.hint: Look at what Ranke says the Jesuits did in schools and in the confessional.

practice.stem: Which evidence does Ranke use to support his claim about the success of the Jesuit schools?

options.A: Figures on the number of Protestants who returned to the Catholic Church in each year
options.B: Letters from several popes praising the work of the Jesuits in Italy and Spain
options.C: Complaints from Protestant teachers who had lost their students to Jesuit schools
options.D: A Jesuit's claim that cardinals and officials had studied in Jesuit schools

practice.explanation: Ranke quotes Orlandini, a Jesuit. Orlandini says many men "robed in the purple of a cardinal" once sat "on the benches of our schools." A careful reader should notice that this proof comes from a member of the order itself.

whyNot.A: Ranke gives no numbers of converts in this passage.
whyNot.B: Ranke does not quote any pope here.
whyNot.C: Ranke does not quote Protestant teachers. He quotes Orlandini, a Jesuit.

practice.hint: Whose words does Ranke quote, and what do they claim?

practice.stem: Jesuit work like that Ranke describes most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: The spread of Calvinism in Scotland
options.B: Permission for Catholic priests to marry
options.C: A Catholic revival in Poland, Bohemia, and Austria
options.D: The closing of Catholic universities in Spain

practice.explanation: Many nobles in Poland, Austria, and Bohemia had become Protestant. Jesuit schools, preachers, and confessors helped bring much of these lands back to the Catholic Church. Catholic rulers often backed their work.

whyNot.A: Calvinism spread in Scotland in spite of Catholic efforts, and the Scottish Parliament broke with the pope in 1560.
whyNot.B: The Council of Trent kept the rule that Catholic priests must not marry.
whyNot.D: The Jesuits founded many colleges and universities. Catholic higher education grew in this period.

practice.hint: Did Jesuit work help Protestant or Catholic churches grow?

practice.stem: Both sources support which of the following claims about witch trials?

options.A: Most accusations began with careful investigations carried out by trained judges.
options.B: Church courts in Protestant lands held most of the trials described.
options.C: Accused witches were usually set free once they had confessed.
options.D: Torture made accused people confess and name others.

practice.explanation: Junius says he confessed and named people only because of the torture. Spee says that a woman who confesses "under stress of pain" is "compelled to accuse others." Witch trials took place in Catholic and Protestant lands alike.

whyNot.A: Spee says trials begin with "superstition, envy, calumnies" and that "proof of the scandal is never asked."
whyNot.B: Both sources describe Catholic German lands. Spee says these problems are worst "among Catholics."
whyNot.C: Junius writes that he has made the confession "for which I must die."

practice.hint: Compare why Junius confessed and named people with what Spee says happens to a woman after torture.

practice.stem: Taken together, the sources best support which conclusion about who was accused of witchcraft?

options.A: Accusations fell mainly on wealthy merchants whose property officials hoped to seize.
options.B: Accusations fell mainly on Protestants who lived in the lands ruled by Catholic prince-bishops.
options.C: Accusations often fell first on poor women but could also reach men of high rank.
options.D: Accusations fell mainly on healers and midwives who practiced folk medicine.

practice.explanation: Across Europe, about three out of four people put to death for witchcraft were women, and many were poor or old. But in big witch hunts, like those at Bamberg and Würzburg, powerful men such as mayors were accused too.

whyNot.A: Spee says the "poor and helpless" woman is the first to suffer, so wealth was not the main target, even though some rich people like Junius were caught up.
whyNot.B: Neither source says the accused were Protestants. The charge was making a pact with the Devil, not holding Protestant beliefs.
whyNot.D: Neither source mentions healing. Spee says rumor and "envy" could point to almost anyone, starting with poor women.

practice.hint: Who does Spee say suffers first? Who was Junius?

practice.stem: Spee's criticism of trials based on rumor and of confessions forced by torture is most similar to the later arguments of which person?

options.A: James VI and I
options.B: Cesare Beccaria
options.C: Cardinal Richelieu
options.D: Philip II of Spain

practice.explanation: In 1764 the Italian writer Cesare Beccaria argued that torture leads to false confessions and should be ended. Spee had made a similar argument more than 100 years earlier.

whyNot.A: King James VI of Scotland (later James I of England) wrote Daemonologie (1597), a book that supported witch hunting.
whyNot.C: Cardinal Richelieu ran France's government for the king from 1624 to 1642. He is known for making royal power stronger, not for criticizing trials.
whyNot.D: Philip II of Spain supported the Spanish Inquisition's harsh treatment of people accused of heresy.

practice.hint: Which person wrote about criminal justice during the Enlightenment?

practice.stem: Which feature of the painting is most typical of Mannerism?

options.A: the stretched bodies and crowded, unreal space of the upper half
options.B: the calm, balanced arrangement of figures based on classical models
options.C: the everyday scene of peasants at work in the countryside
options.D: the careful use of one-point perspective to create a realistic and orderly room

practice.explanation: Mannerist painters such as El Greco stretched bodies and bent space to create a strange, spiritual feeling. The tall, thin figures and swirling heaven in this painting are good examples.

whyNot.B: Balance and classical calm mark High Renaissance art, such as Raphael's. El Greco crowds his figures together and stretches them.
whyNot.C: There are no peasants or fields here. The painting shows a burial and a vision of heaven.
whyNot.D: El Greco does not build a realistic room with one-point perspective. Heaven and earth are stacked in a flat, crowded space.

practice.hint: Look at the shapes of the bodies in the top half. Do they look natural?

practice.stem: Given its subject and the church it was made for, the painting was most likely intended to

options.A: support the Council of Trent's teaching on saints and good works
options.B: support the Protestant teaching that people are saved by faith alone
options.C: celebrate Spain's naval victory over the Ottoman Turks at Lepanto
options.D: show the hardships of ordinary people during Europe's wars of religion in the 1500s

practice.explanation: The Council of Trent taught that saints in heaven help living people and that good works matter for salvation. This painting shows saints honoring a man who gave gifts to the very church it was made for.

whyNot.B: Spain was firmly Catholic. The painting shows saints honoring a man who gave to the Church, a kind of good work that Protestants said could not earn salvation.
whyNot.C: The Battle of Lepanto (1571) was a sea battle. The painting shows a funeral and a vision of heaven, with no ships or war.
whyNot.D: The figures are churchmen, nobles, and saints in rich clothing, not ordinary people suffering from war.

practice.hint: According to the legend in the caption, why did the saints come down from heaven?

practice.stem: Compared with High Renaissance paintings such as Raphael's The School of Athens, this painting places greater emphasis on

options.A: balance, harmony, and calm, ideal proportions
options.B: distortion and intense spiritual feeling
options.C: ancient Greek and Roman philosophers
options.D: realistic scenes of everyday life

practice.explanation: High Renaissance art stressed balance and perfect proportions. Mannerists such as El Greco stretched figures and crowded the space to stir strong religious feeling.

whyNot.A: Balance and calm proportions are what Raphael's The School of Athens stresses most.
whyNot.C: Raphael's The School of Athens shows ancient philosophers. El Greco shows saints, angels, and a funeral.
whyNot.D: Neither painting shows everyday life. For that, think of Bruegel's peasant scenes.

practice.hint: Think about how El Greco's figures differ from the calm figures of the early 1500s.

practice.stem: Vives's main proposal is that the city government should

options.A: register the poor and put all who are able to work into jobs
options.B: leave the care of the poor to monasteries and private charity
options.C: allow beggars to collect gifts freely on the steps of churches
options.D: give poor families a weekly payment without asking them to work

practice.explanation: Vives wanted the city council to list the poor, find out why they were poor, and give jobs to those able to work. This was part of a new trend: city governments, not only the Church, began to organize help for the poor.

whyNot.B: Vives wants "two Senators for each parish" to register the poor, so the city, not the monasteries, takes charge.
whyNot.C: Vives wants beggars examined and put to work. He complains that children "bring home more from begging."
whyNot.D: Vives says that no one fit for work should "be idle." Help depends on working if one can.

practice.hint: What does Vives want the "Senators" to do, and what does he say about being idle?

practice.stem: Vives's proposal is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Henry VIII's closing of the monasteries in England and the loss of the charity they gave
options.B: the first arrival of the plague in Europe and the death of many workers
options.C: growing numbers of beggars in the commercial cities of the 1500s
options.D: the destruction of Flemish towns during the Thirty Years' War

practice.explanation: In the early 1500s, a growing population, rising prices, and wars pushed many poor country people into trading cities like Bruges. City leaders faced crowds of beggars and began to plan help for the poor.

whyNot.A: Henry VIII closed the English monasteries in 1536–1540, ten years after Vives wrote, and in a different country.
whyNot.B: The Black Death first struck Europe in 1347, almost two centuries earlier.
whyNot.D: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, long after 1526.

practice.hint: What was happening to cities and the number of poor people in the early 1500s?

practice.stem: Plans like Vives's are most similar to which later English law?

options.A: The Act of Supremacy of 1534
options.B: The Navigation Acts
options.C: The Corn Laws
options.D: The Elizabethan Poor Law of 1601

practice.explanation: England's Poor Law of 1601 made each parish collect a tax to help the poor. It set people who could work to work and punished idle beggars. Like Vives's plan, it made local government responsible for the poor.

whyNot.A: The Act of Supremacy made Henry VIII head of the Church of England. It did not deal with the poor.
whyNot.B: The Navigation Acts (from 1651) required trade with England's colonies to be carried in English ships.
whyNot.C: The Corn Laws (best known from the law of 1815) taxed imported grain to protect the profits of English landowners.

practice.hint: Which law made local officials responsible for people like those Vives describes?

exam.title: Unit 2 Practice Exam: Age of Reformation
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of European history from c. 1450 to c. 1648. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or words for groups of people that are no longer used; these words show the language of their time.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 rejects the authority of Scripture, while Source 2 treats Scripture as the highest religious authority.
options.B: Source 1 uses the gospel against serfdom, while Source 2 says it cannot justify revolt.
options.C: Source 1 calls for overthrowing the princes, while Source 2 calls for peasants to elect their own lords.
options.D: Source 1 asks for Catholic worship to be restored, while Source 2 defends new Protestant worship.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The peasants appeal to Scripture throughout and promise to drop any article that is "against the word of God."
rationales.B: Correct. The peasants say Christ "redeemed us all" and that freedom is "consistent with Scripture." Luther answers that the rebels "cloak" their sins "with the gospel."
rationales.C: Incorrect. The peasants say they do not want to be "absolutely free and under no authority," and Luther demands obedience to rulers, not elections.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The peasants want pastors who teach "the gospel pure and simple," a Reformation demand, not a return to Catholic worship.

questions.explanation: The peasants argue that serfdom goes against Scripture because Christ "redeemed us all." Luther answers that the rebels "cloak" their sins "with the gospel." He says that "whosoever can" should strike them down.

questions.stem: Source 1 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: English landlords fencing off open fields to raise sheep for the growing trade in wool
options.B: Catholic bishops collecting new taxes to pay for the Council of Trent
options.C: armies of the Thirty Years' War plundering villages across the Holy Roman Empire
options.D: German lords raising peasants' dues and taking control of common lands and woods

rationales.A: Incorrect. Enclosure for sheep farming was mainly an English development. The Twelve Articles come from southern Germany.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Council of Trent did not meet until 1545, twenty years after the Twelve Articles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, almost a century after 1525.
rationales.D: Correct. In the early 1500s many German lords demanded more dues and labor and claimed meadows, woods, and fishing rights. Reformation preaching gave peasants new arguments against them.

questions.explanation: In the early 1500s, German lords made peasants pay more and work more. Lords also took over woods, streams, and shared fields. Reformation preaching gave peasants new reasons to protest, and revolts spread in 1524–1525.

questions.stem: Members of which group would most strongly have supported the argument in Source 2?

options.A: Swabian peasants
options.B: Followers of Thomas Müntzer
options.C: German princes and nobles
options.D: Anabaptist congregations

rationales.A: Incorrect. Luther calls the rebels "mad dogs" and says their Twelve Articles were "all vain pretense."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Thomas Müntzer, a radical preacher, led rebels in Thuringia in 1525. Luther attacked him, and the princes executed him after the rebels' defeat.
rationales.C: Correct. Luther says that "whosoever can" should "smite, strangle, and stab" the rebels. The princes and nobles wanted to hear this.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Anabaptists taught that Christians should not use the sword, so they rejected Luther's call to kill rebels.

questions.explanation: Luther said that "whosoever can" should strike down the rebels. German princes and nobles did so, killing tens of thousands of peasants in 1525.

questions.stem: The events of 1525 described in the sources contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: The Peace of Augsburg's grant of religious freedom to peasants
options.B: The end of serfdom in the German states by the 1550s
options.C: Princes' growing control over Lutheran churches
options.D: The Catholic Church's decision to let parishes elect their priests

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each prince, not each peasant, choose the religion of his land.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Serfdom lasted in many German lands until the 1800s.
rationales.C: Correct. After 1525 Luther and his followers relied on princes to protect and organize Lutheran churches. Many princes became heads of the churches in their lands.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Catholic Church kept bishops in charge of appointing priests.

questions.explanation: After the Peasants' War, Luther and his followers relied on princes to set up and run Lutheran churches. In many German states the prince became head of the church. This gave the state more control over religion.

questions.stem: Luther's call to "smite, strangle, and stab" rebels contrasts most strongly with the views of which group?

options.A: Anabaptists
options.B: Calvinists
options.C: Anglicans
options.D: Lutheran princes

rationales.A: Correct. Many Anabaptists, such as those who met at Schleitheim in 1527, taught that Christians must not use the sword or serve as rulers or soldiers.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Calvin taught that rulers hold the sword from God to punish wrongdoers, much as Luther did.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Church of England was headed by the monarch, and it supported royal power to punish rebels.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Lutheran princes followed Luther's advice and used force to crush the peasants' revolt.

questions.explanation: Luther believed that God gave rulers the sword to keep order. Many Anabaptists said Christians should not use the sword at all. This is one reason both Catholic and Protestant rulers persecuted them.

questions.stem: Calvin most likely wrote the letter in order to

options.A: ask the king to make Calvin's teachings the official religion of the French kingdom
options.B: urge French Protestants to take up arms against the king's officials
options.C: show the king that Protestants were loyal subjects, not rebels
options.D: apologize to the king for teachings that Calvin now admitted were wrong

rationales.A: Incorrect. Calvin defends Protestant teaching and protests the persecution. He does not ask the king to make it France's religion.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Calvin presents Protestants as loyal, peaceful subjects. He does not call for armed resistance.
rationales.C: Correct. Calvin protests that his teachings are falsely accused of aiming to "subvert all orders and civil governments" and of troubling "the peace and quiet of the people."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Here "apology" means a written defense. Calvin defends his teaching as the true gospel and takes none of it back.

questions.explanation: After 1534 French Protestants were being jailed and burned. Calvin wanted to show Francis I that their faith was the old gospel of Paul, not a plot to overthrow kings.

questions.stem: The conflict Calvin describes contributed most directly to which later development in France?

options.A: The Fronde
options.B: The French Wars of Religion
options.C: The Concordat of Bologna
options.D: The War of the Spanish Succession

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Fronde (1648–1653) was a revolt of nobles and judges against royal power, not a religious war.
rationales.B: Correct. Calvinism spread among French nobles and townspeople, who became known as Huguenots. Conflict between Huguenots and Catholics led to the French Wars of Religion (1562–1598).
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Concordat of Bologna (1516) gave the French king the right to name bishops. It came before Calvin's letter.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) was fought over who would inherit Spain's throne.

questions.explanation: In the 1540s and 1550s, Calvin's ideas spread in France, especially among nobles and townspeople. These French Protestants were called Huguenots. Fighting between Huguenots and Catholics became the French Wars of Religion (1562–1598).

questions.stem: To answer the charge that Protestant teaching is new, Calvin argues that it

options.A: restores the faith that Paul and the first Christians taught
options.B: was approved by many bishops at a recent church council
options.C: had already been accepted by many princes and free cities in Germany
options.D: follows the writings of ancient Greek and Roman philosophers

rationales.A: Correct. Calvin says those who "know the preaching of Paul to be old" will "find nothing new among us."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Calvin does not mention a council or any bishops' approval. He appeals to Scripture.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Calvin does not point to princes or cities that accepted Protestant teaching. He points to Paul and to Christ.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Calvin points to Paul and Christ, not to Greek or Roman philosophers.

questions.explanation: Protestant reformers said they were bringing back the Christianity of the Bible. Calvin says that people who know Paul's preaching will find "nothing new" in Protestant teaching.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Gustavus's reasons for entering the war, as he presents them?

options.A: Winning new colonies and trading posts for Sweden in the Americas
options.B: Restoring the pope's authority in northern Germany
options.C: Carrying out the orders of the Holy Roman Emperor
options.D: Defending fellow Protestants and Sweden's own security

rationales.A: Incorrect. Sweden's small American colony, New Sweden, was not founded until 1638. Gustavus speaks of enemies around the Baltic Sea.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Gustavus fights against the emperor, who he says wants the Protestant faith "wholly rooted out."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Gustavus fights against "the emperor and his followers."
rationales.D: Correct. Gustavus says the emperor wants "the evangelical religion" rooted out, and he also says he seeks "the security of my kingdom."

questions.explanation: Gustavus says the emperor wants to root out "the evangelical religion." He also wants "the security of my kingdom," since his enemies had attacked him. For Gustavus, faith and Sweden's own safety went together.

questions.stem: Which Catholic power paid subsidies to support Sweden's war against the Habsburg emperor, showing that the war was not only about religion?

options.A: Spain
options.B: Bavaria
options.C: Poland
options.D: France

rationales.A: Incorrect. Spain was ruled by a branch of the Habsburg family and fought on the emperor's side.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Maximilian, the Catholic duke of Bavaria, led the Catholic League. He fought on the emperor's side.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Catholic Poland had fought Sweden in the 1620s and was its rival around the Baltic Sea.
rationales.D: Correct. Under Cardinal Richelieu, Catholic France agreed in 1631 to pay Sweden to fight the Habsburgs, and in 1635 France entered the war itself.

questions.explanation: Cardinal Richelieu, France's chief minister, cared more about weakening the Habsburgs than about religion. In 1631 Catholic France agreed to pay Protestant Sweden to keep fighting. In 1635 France itself joined the war against the Habsburgs.

questions.stem: The war Gustavus describes ended with a peace settlement that

options.A: restored Catholic unity across the Holy Roman Empire under the emperor
options.B: broke up the Holy Roman Empire into independent nation-states
options.C: recognized Calvinism and confirmed princes' control of religion in their lands
options.D: made Lutheranism the single official religion of the entire Holy Roman Empire

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Peace of Westphalia accepted the religious split in the empire. It ended hopes of restoring Catholic unity.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Holy Roman Empire lasted until 1806. The peace gave its princes more power, but it did not end the empire.
rationales.C: Correct. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) added Calvinism to the faiths a ruler could follow and confirmed the princes' control over religion in their own lands.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The peace kept Catholic, Lutheran, and Calvinist states side by side. No single church became official everywhere.

questions.explanation: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) made Calvinism a legal faith next to Catholicism and Lutheranism. It gave the empire's princes more control over religion and over their own lands. Sweden and France gained territory.

questions.stem: The decrees were most directly a response to which Protestant idea?

options.A: that God has already chosen which people will be saved and which will not
options.B: that monasteries should be closed and their lands sold for the public good
options.C: that Scripture alone, without church tradition, is the source of religious truth
options.D: that the bread of the Lord's Supper does not become the body of Christ

rationales.A: Incorrect. These decrees deal with which books and traditions carry God's truth and who may interpret them, not with who will be saved.
rationales.B: Incorrect. These decrees say nothing about monasteries.
rationales.C: Correct. Luther and other reformers said Scripture alone was the final authority. The Council answered that God's truth is found in Scripture and in "unwritten traditions."
rationales.D: Incorrect. These decrees are about Scripture, tradition, and printing, not about the Lord's Supper.

questions.explanation: Protestants said Scripture alone had the final say, and that believers could read it for themselves. The Council answered that truth is found in Scripture and in "unwritten traditions." It also said that only "holy mother Church" may judge what Scripture truly means.

questions.stem: The decree on printers is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: the spread of religious pamphlets made possible by printing
options.B: the Church's condemnation of Galileo's writings about the earth's motion around the sun
options.C: the Renaissance popes' spending on art and buildings in Rome
options.D: Ferdinand and Isabella's expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492

rationales.A: Correct. By 1546 printers across Europe were turning out Bibles, books about Scripture, and pamphlets, many without an author's name. Protestant ideas spread through print.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Galileo was condemned in 1633, almost ninety years after this decree.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Papal building projects did not lead to rules about printers. The decree targets religious books printed without church approval.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The expulsion of Spain's Jews in 1492 was a royal order about religion in Spain. It had nothing to do with printed books.

questions.explanation: Printed books and pamphlets spread Protestant ideas quickly. So the Council ruled that a bishop had to approve religious books before they could be sold. It also banned religious books printed without the author's name.

questions.stem: Which later Catholic measure most directly continued the policy in the decree on printers?

options.A: The Edict of Nantes
options.B: The Peace of Augsburg
options.C: The Index of Prohibited Books
options.D: The Concordat of 1801

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Edict of Nantes (1598) was a French royal decree that gave Protestants the right to worship. It was not a church rule about books.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let German princes choose Catholicism or Lutheranism. It was not about books.
rationales.C: Correct. The papacy issued the Index, a list of books Catholics were forbidden to read, in 1559, and a revised Index followed the Council of Trent in 1564.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Napoleon's Concordat with the pope (1801) dealt with relations between church and state in France.

questions.explanation: In 1559 the pope issued the Index of Prohibited Books, a list of books Catholics were not allowed to read. A new Index came out in 1564, after the Council of Trent.

questions.stem: Which of the following most likely contributed to the rise in witchcraft trials in 1638–1657 compared with 1618–1637?

options.A: The Spanish Inquisition
options.B: The Scientific Revolution
options.C: Elizabeth I's witchcraft law
options.D: The English Civil War

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Spanish Inquisition never worked in England, and these trials were held in the king's courts.
rationales.B: Incorrect. New scientific ideas later helped make educated people doubt witchcraft, which lowered the number of trials.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Elizabeth I's witchcraft law dates from 1563, long before this rise.
rationales.D: Correct. During the English Civil War (1642–1651), normal government broke down and fear ran high. In 1645 Matthew Hopkins led a witch hunt in Essex.

questions.explanation: During the English Civil War (1642–1651), courts and local government were disrupted and fear ran high. In 1645 Matthew Hopkins led a witch hunt in Essex, and 22 people were hanged in 1638–1647, the most of any decade in the chart.

questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data?

options.A: Witchcraft trials in these courts rose steadily from 1558 to 1707.
options.B: Most people indicted for witchcraft in these courts were not hanged.
options.C: More people were hanged in 1588–1597 than in any other decade.
options.D: Witchcraft trials in these courts stopped in the 1660s.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Trials peaked in 1578–1597, fell, rose again in 1638–1657, and then dropped almost to zero.
rationales.B: Correct. In every decade fewer people were hanged than were indicted. In all, 513 people were indicted and 112 were hanged.
rationales.C: Incorrect. More people were hanged in 1638–1647 (22) than in 1588–1597 (18).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Trials continued after the 1660s in small numbers, until 1698–1707.

questions.explanation: In every decade fewer people were hanged than were indicted. Of the 513 people indicted, 112 were hanged, so about four out of five escaped hanging.

questions.stem: The painting is most clearly an example of which artistic style?

options.A: Mannerism
options.B: Baroque
options.C: Neoclassicism
options.D: Romanticism

rationales.A: Incorrect. Mannerist painters such as El Greco stretched figures and flattened space in strange ways. Rubens's figures are full and natural, set in a deep space.
rationales.B: Correct. Baroque painters such as Rubens used rich color, crowds of figures, movement, and drama to impress viewers, often for royal or church patrons.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Neoclassical art of the late 1700s, such as Jacques-Louis David's, used simple settings and stern scenes from ancient Rome.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Romantic art of the early 1800s stressed wild nature, intense personal feeling, and national struggles.

questions.explanation: Rubens was the leading Baroque painter of northern Europe. His crowded, colorful, dramatic scenes were made to impress people. They showed the power and glory of the rulers and churches that paid him.

questions.stem: Given its subject and the person who ordered it, the painting was most likely intended to

options.A: glorify Marie de' Medici and strengthen her authority as queen
options.B: criticize the French royal court for its wealth and luxury
options.C: record a royal ceremony exactly as it happened, for a palace archive
options.D: persuade French Catholics to accept Protestant forms of worship

rationales.A: Correct. Marie de' Medici ordered the series of paintings to celebrate her life and her right to rule as queen and regent after her husband's death.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Rubens painted the series for Marie herself, so it praises the court instead of criticizing it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rubens arranged the scene to flatter the queen. Such paintings were meant to impress, not to be exact records.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The painting honors a Catholic ceremony, with bishops and cardinals taking part. It does not promote Protestant worship.

questions.explanation: In 1622 Marie de' Medici hired Rubens to paint 24 large pictures for her palace in Paris. Most show scenes from her life. Like many Baroque works paid for by rulers, they were meant to show her power and glory.

questions.stem: King Henry IV of France, who watches from the balcony in the painting, is best known for which of the following?

options.A: Signing the Peace of Augsburg
options.B: Issuing the Edict of Nantes
options.C: Passing the Act of Supremacy
options.D: Issuing the Edict of Worms

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) was made in the Holy Roman Empire, under Emperor Charles V's brother Ferdinand.
rationales.B: Correct. In 1598 Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes, which gave French Protestants the right to worship in many places and ended the French Wars of Religion.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Act of Supremacy (1534) was an English law that made Henry VIII head of the Church of England.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Edict of Worms (1521) was Emperor Charles V's decree against Martin Luther.

questions.explanation: Henry IV was a Protestant who became Catholic to win the French throne. In 1598 he issued the Edict of Nantes, which allowed Huguenots to worship in many places and ended the French Wars of Religion. He was murdered in 1610.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Luther's view of women in the passage?

options.A: Women's chief role is to be wives and mothers who manage the household.
options.B: Women should share equally with men in governing the church and state.
options.C: Women should enter convents instead of marrying, to keep themselves pure.
options.D: Women understand Scripture better than men and should teach in churches.

rationales.A: Correct. Luther says women should "keep house, and bear and bring up children," and he gives his wife command only "in all household matters."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Luther says "Never any good came out of female domination" and keeps his own rights "in other points."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Luther praises marriage as "the chief in the world after religion" and attacks the forbidding of marriage.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Luther claims men have "more understanding than the women."

questions.explanation: Luther praised marriage and gave wives authority at home. But he believed women were made mainly "to bear children" and to "keep house," and he kept public authority for men.

questions.stem: Luther's views on marriage differed most from Catholic teaching of his time in that Luther

options.A: taught that marriage was one of seven sacraments administered by priests
options.B: allowed priests to marry if they first received special permission from the pope
options.C: insisted that monks and nuns keep their vows of lifelong chastity
options.D: rejected required celibacy for clergy and praised marriage as God's plan for all

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Catholic Church counted marriage as one of seven sacraments. Luther did not count marriage as a sacrament, though he honored it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Luther rejected the pope's authority. He says forbidding marriage is a sign of "God's enmity to Popedom."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Luther urged monks and nuns to leave their vows and marry. In 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a former nun.
rationales.D: Correct. The Catholic Church required priests, monks, and nuns to stay unmarried. Luther calls forbidding marriage, "a law of nature," a sign of "God's enmity to Popedom."

questions.explanation: The Catholic Church did not let priests, monks, or nuns marry. Luther said marriage is "a law of nature." Banning it was like telling people not "to eat, to drink, to sleep." Protestant pastors married and had families.

questions.stem: A historian studying the daily lives of married women in Lutheran towns would find the passage limited mainly because it

options.A: gives a male reformer's opinions, not women's own experiences
options.B: was recorded before the Protestant Reformation had begun in Germany
options.C: describes Catholic marriage customs rather than Lutheran ones
options.D: was written as a law that Lutheran families in Wittenberg were required to obey

rationales.A: Correct. The remarks show what one Protestant leader thought women should be. To learn about women's actual lives, a historian would need sources such as women's letters, court records, and household accounts.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Luther made these remarks in the 1530s and 1540s, years after the Reformation had begun.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Luther describes his own marriage and his own beliefs as a Protestant reformer.
rationales.D: Incorrect. These were remarks at dinner, not a law. They show opinions, not rules that were enforced.

questions.explanation: The passage shows what one leading reformer believed about women and marriage. It does not show how women in Lutheran towns actually lived, worked, or thought.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Weber's main argument?

options.A: Catholic teaching about charity to the poor was the main cause of the growth of European capitalism.
options.B: The growth of capitalism caused Europeans to give up religion in favor of making money.
options.C: Protestants grew rich mainly because their rulers gave them the lands taken from the Church.
options.D: Calvinist anxiety about salvation encouraged hard work and saving, which helped capitalism grow.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Weber links capitalism to Protestant ideas and notes that business leaders were "overwhelmingly Protestant."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Weber argues the other way around: religious ideas encouraged "the spirit of capitalism."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Some Protestant rulers did take Church lands, but Weber's argument is about religious attitudes toward work and saving.
rationales.D: Correct. Weber says the question "Am I one of the elect?" led believers to "intense worldly activity," and that saving led to the "accumulation of capital."

questions.explanation: Weber says Calvinists worried about whether they were "one of the elect." Hard work seemed to show that God had chosen them. They also spent little and saved a lot, and that saved money helped businesses grow.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most challenge Weber's argument?

options.A: Calvinist merchants in the Dutch Republic built one of Europe's richest trading economies during the 1600s.
options.B: Banking and trade flourished in Catholic cities such as Florence and Venice before the Reformation.
options.C: Puritan preachers in England urged believers to work hard at the jobs God had called them to.
options.D: Calvinist church courts in Geneva punished people for laziness and wasteful spending.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Dutch Calvinist wealth fits Weber's argument, so it supports rather than challenges it.
rationales.B: Correct. If capitalism was already strong in Catholic cities such as Florence and Venice in the 1300s and 1400s, then Protestant ideas cannot be its main cause.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Puritan preaching about hard work in a calling is the kind of evidence Weber uses to support his argument.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Punishing laziness and waste fits Weber's claim that Calvinists valued discipline and saving.

questions.explanation: Weber ties the rise of capitalism to Protestant ideas. But the Medici bankers of Florence and the merchants of Venice ran big businesses long before the Reformation. Many historians use this fact to argue against Weber.

questions.stem: The growth of capitalism that Weber discusses is best understood in the context of which development of the 1500s and 1600s?

options.A: The expansion of overseas trade and banking
options.B: The closing of Mediterranean trade
options.C: A return to self-sufficient manors
options.D: The rise of steam-powered factories

rationales.A: Correct. In the 1500s and 1600s Europe's commercial economy grew. Antwerp and later Amsterdam became centers of trade, banking, and joint-stock companies such as the Dutch East India Company (1602).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mediterranean trade continued, and trade across the Atlantic and with Asia grew quickly in this period.
rationales.C: Incorrect. After the Black Death, money payments and markets spread, and Europe moved further away from self-sufficient manors.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Steam-powered factories came with the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain after about 1760.

questions.explanation: In the 1500s and 1600s, trade with the Americas and Asia made cities like Antwerp and Amsterdam rich. New banks and trading companies, such as the Dutch East India Company (1602), helped business grow.
